rv.q: More than a tribute, it’s a feast — and one of the most heartfelt and joyous shows of the season.

That lush and emotional all-company song, called “Sunday,” is one of 42 numbers in “Old Friends,” a supremely entertaining and altogether divine celebration of Sondheim’s legacy created by producer Cameron Mackintosh that opened Tuesday at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre.
The headliners are wonderfully showcased.
Indeed, this whole crew was mostly in the original creative kitchens; I say, catch ‘em while you still can.
Others are middling, a few are misfires.

You can’t take offense at the concept — it accomplishes exactly what it aims to do, which is to remind you that Sondheim wrote some really great songs — but you do start to fantasize about it all slowing down and just committing to the dramatic frames that contained them.
Perhaps fittingly, the best reason to see Old Friends is the oldest thing in it: Bernadette Peters.
What’s on display is unmitigatedly glorious.
As its title suggests, this is a classy, comfortable pair of slippers—or the warmest, most luxurious musical bubble bath a Sondheim fan could wish for.
The ebullient Old Friends is loaded with vocal talent that can move mountains.
Bernadette Peters – of course! – and Lea Salonga lead a cast of talented singers and hoofers, who make the most of this opportunity to shine.
All I can say is, it's your time; breathe it in and enjoy the ride.
Once you accept the show's limited ambitions, as I gradually did over the course of this pleasant and jauntily staged musical revue, you can let yourself to have a good time.
These are talented performers putting over some tuneful and clever numbers, in what is the latest of many Sondheim revues – which have their obvious pleasures, as well as some potential pitfalls.
But the cavalcade of winning numbers is more than infrequently interrupted by items which do not quite add to the evening’s enjoyment, serving to deplete the showmanship of the whole.
The result feels more like a mixtape than a tribute, more exhausting than illuminating.
Others are, and this revue does not do them justice.
It's gloriously delicious, akin to 'Being Alive' with some Old Friends, 'Side by Side.'

Old Friends is a beautiful snapshot of all things Sondheim and a loving tribute that holds space for all of the themes he explored and the space between loneliness and a whole world that’s having fun just out of reach.
It’s a delight to hear even a few dozen of them, produced so artfully in a production that doesn’t stint on visual showmanship.
Director Matthew Bourne provides an uneven evening and a song order that doesn’t completely make sense.
Despite powerhouse leading ladies Bernadette Peters and Lea Salonga, 'Sondheim's Old Friends' sometimes forgets what made the master great.

cn.t: A lavish, star-studded tribute featuring Bernadette Peters and Lea Salonga earns praise for its talented ensemble and fully-staged numbers, though critics are divided on whether Broadway needs another Sondheim revue, with some finding it overlong.

vr.q: That was so good and so beautiful and what a fantastic tribute. If you will have a chance to see this in New York, go.
I could watch this again and again and again and it boggles my mind that this isn't a one night only concert... that's how special this thing was
I did not expect to be emotionally destroyed by Old Friends on Broadway, but in retrospect, I really should have known better.
Any excuse to hear excellent performers sing the music of Steven Sonheime, I'm there. I'm happy to buy a ticket and see that and I was not disappointed by that at all.
